items.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023
items.q: Like Ravel had his shit together and then we’re all still playing the chord changes that we like

ctx.x: Let me go back a bit — you said improvising is a mysterious art — a mysterious thing to do. When you play a solo, an improvised solo over a one or two chord vamp or a 12-bar blues, is what’s going on in your head different than what you would play on “Giant Steps”? Or even “Body and Soul.” In other words more chord changes — how do you negotiate the challenging chord changes of a song as opposed to a one chord vamp?

Each of them presents their own challenges. The thing about playing over one chord is to not resort to hot licks, you know, modal patterns and stuff that you practiced. And I think so much of it just depends on the players you’re playing with. If you’re playing with creative players then somehow you’re being presented with alternate pathways or suggestions or prompts or opportunities to go different places you know. And, or you could play something that they respond to and that leads you to another place. Playing…

I liked what you said about the theory coming after the creativity. Every once in a while I put on Cannonball’s, one of his very first records with Miles was on it, and they played “Autumn Leaves.” And the solo that Cannonball plays is utterly fascinating. And he’s got all these sort of not-in-the-chord tones, but the way he fashions them I’m just in awe.
